title: When Does Global Rationality Exist? A Representation Theory for Evaluative Systems
content: Architecture-dependent systems pose a fundamental local-to-global problem in which locally admissible and locally evaluated changes need not admit a globally coherent scalar representation. This paper develops a systems-theoretic framework for determining when such local evaluations can be integrated into a global scalar measure. The framework combines system state and architecture, admissible directions of change, local evaluation, and induced dynamics within a differential-geometric structure. The main result establishes a local-to-global representation theorem. Under connectedness and bracket generation, a global scalar representation exists if and only if the horizontal evaluation form has zero circulation along every closed horizontal curve, equivalently, if horizontal evaluation is path independent. When it exists, the representation is unique up to an additive constant and reproduces the primitive canonical rational correspondence exactly. Along every canonical rational trajectory, its rate of change equals the maximal local evaluative rate. Under additional regularity, feasible inaction, and precompactness conditions, this identity yields strict ascent outside the rational-equilibrium set, excludes non-equilibrium recurrence, and confines limiting behaviour to rational equilibria. The results establish that global objective, potential, or performance functions cannot in general be imposed independently of system architecture. Their existence is determined by the integrability of the underlying architecture-dependent evaluative geometry.
